title: Breathings and accents

objectives.can: Read rough and smooth breathings and name the acute, grave and circumflex accents.

explanation.summary: A printed Greek text carries small marks over its vowels: a breathing on the first vowel of many words, and an accent on one syllable of most words. You must know them to read a word aloud, and a few pairs of words differ only in these marks.

sections.heading: Breathings: with h or without
body: Every word that begins with a vowel or a diphthong has a breathing on that first vowel. The smooth breathing shows that there is no h before the vowel. The rough breathing shows that there is: the word is read as if an h came first. So ἐν is read 'en' and ὁ is read 'ho'.

A word that begins with υ always has a rough breathing, as in ὑποκάτω. A word that begins with ρ also has a rough breathing, as in ῥῆμα, and the Latin-letter spelling shows it as rh. No other consonant carries a breathing.

On a diphthong the breathing stands on the second vowel, not the first: οὗτος, αὐτός, εἰς, οἱ. On a capital the mark stands before the letter: Ἐν, Ἀβραάμ. A capital diphthong keeps the mark on its second vowel, as in Οὐκ.

sections.heading: Three accents
body: The acute accent (ά) can stand on any one of the last three syllables of a word. The circumflex (ᾶ) can stand only on one of the last two syllables, and only on a long vowel or a diphthong: it stands on the ω of φῶς and on the ι of εἶ. The grave accent (ὰ) can stand only on the last syllable.

The grave replaces an acute on the last syllable when another word follows with no punctuation between. So θεός becomes θεὸς in 'God was the Word', where ἦν follows, but keeps its acute in θεόν when a comma follows. A few words, such as the question word τίς, keep the acute even before another word.

In the ancient language the accent was a rise of pitch. In the school convention it is read as stress on the marked syllable, and lesson G0.3.1 says how to find the syllable. The authors of the New Testament did not write breathings or accents; later copyists and editors added them as an aid to reading.

sections.heading: Marks that tell words apart
body: A few words differ only by a mark. τίς with an acute is the question 'who?' and τις without an accent is the indefinite 'someone' or 'a certain'. εἰ is 'if' and εἶ is 'you are'. ὁ is the article 'the' and ὅ is the relative 'which'. ἡ is the article, ἤ is 'or' and ἦν is 'was'. Look at the mark before you decide what you are reading.

sections.heading: Punctuation
body: Editions print four marks. The comma (,) and the full stop (.) are used as in English. The raised dot (·) marks a break stronger than a comma and is used where English would use a colon or semicolon. The question mark (;) looks like an English semicolon and ends a question.
The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation. Editors added these marks, so they sometimes differ from one edition to another.
An apostrophe marks a vowel dropped before a word that begins with a vowel, as in δι’ αὐτοῦ, where διά has lost its final α. This is called elision.

misunderstandings: A breathing is not an accent. It marks whether there is an h. An accent marks the stressed syllable. Words can carry one or both.
Not every word that begins with a vowel has a rough breathing. Many, such as ἐν and ἀρχῇ, have the smooth one.
The grave accent is not a different stress. It is an acute on the last syllable that gives way when another word follows.
The Greek question mark (;) is not an English semicolon. It ends a question.

deeper.heading: Words with no accent of their own
body: A few small words, such as ὁ, ἡ, οἱ, αἱ, ἐν, εἰς and ἐκ, are written without an accent. They lean on the word that follows. Other small words, such as τις, lean on the word before them and sometimes pass their accent to it. Fuller rules for these are part of later grammar. Further rules also decide which accent can stand on which syllable according to the length of the last vowel.

examples.analysis: Ἐν begins with a capital, so its smooth breathing stands before the letter; it is read 'en'. ὁ has a rough breathing and no accent: it is the article, read 'ho'. λόγος has an acute accent on its first syllable, the next-to-last, and no breathing, because it begins with a consonant.

examples.analysis: οὗτος begins with the diphthong ου, so its rough breathing and its circumflex both stand on the second vowel, υ. It is read 'HOU-tos'. ἐν has a smooth breathing. ἀρχῇ has a smooth breathing on α and a circumflex on its last syllable, the long vowel ῃ.

examples.analysis: ζωὴ carries a grave accent on its last syllable because another word, ἦν, follows without punctuation. ἡ is the article with a rough breathing and no accent; it is not ἤ, 'or'. ἀνθρώπων has an acute on the next-to-last syllable. The verse ends with a raised dot, a stop stronger than a comma.

reading.why: A passage of questions and answers, so it has all four marks of punctuation, both breathings (including a capital diphthong), all three accents, and the pairs τίς/τις and εἶ/εἰ in use.
